---
title: Integrating the mesher
description: The meshing calls a program builds on to turn a cadjoint part into a mesh it can draw, check and export.
---

A program that takes cadjoint parts and needs meshes of them, a CAD tool's
viewer or exporter for example, should need one grid, one extraction and two
checks. This page lists those calls and what each one promises. The names
listed here are the stable surface: a patch release does not change them, and
a minor release that does says so in its notes. Everything else in
`cadjoint.meshing` is the pipeline's own stages. Those stages are public for
research and gradients, and they can change between minor releases.

## Example

```python
from cadjoint.meshing import (
    SurfaceOptions, extract_surface, mesh_topology, surface_grid, wall_thickness,
)

grid = surface_grid(part, cell=1.0)            # or bounds=((x0, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z1))
surface = extract_surface(part, SurfaceOptions(feature_edges=True), grid=grid)

if surface.clipped:
    raise ValueError("the bounds cut the part")
topology = mesh_topology(surface.mesh)
if not topology.watertight or topology.bodies != 1:
    raise ValueError(f"{topology.open_edges} open edges, {topology.bodies} bodies")
walls = wall_thickness(part, surface.mesh, surface.cell)
if not walls.resolved:
    raise ValueError(f"thinnest wall {walls.cells:.1f} cells: use a cell of {walls.thinnest / 4:.3g}")

shaded = surface.render_mesh()                 # vertices, normals, faces: a glTF primitive
lines = surface.feature_edges                  # (E, 2, 3) segments: a glTF LINES primitive
```

## The grid

`surface_grid(sdf, resolution=None, *, cell=None, bounds=None)` lays the
lattice. Give it exactly one of these:

- `cell`: the largest cell edge in model units. Each axis takes
  `ceil(extent / cell)` cells, so the box is kept exactly and every spacing is
  at most `cell`.
- `resolution`: the number of cells along the longest axis.

The box comes from `bounds` when the caller gives one. Otherwise
`fit_bounds(sdf)` finds the part at whatever scale it is modelled, by
scanning cubes of half-width 1 to 4096. An empty or unbounded field (a bare
`Plane`, a missing `Intersection`) raises `ValueError`.

The cell decides what the mesh can hold. A wall needs about four cells across
(`WALL_CELLS`) to come out with flat faces at its true thickness. Under about
two (`MIN_WALL_CELLS`) the wall's two faces share cells, so the mesh is
scalloped there, closes through the wall, or falls apart. So the cell to model
a part at is its thinnest wall divided by four. Memory grows with the cube of
the cell count: 256 cells along each axis means 17 million samples.

## The surface

`extract_surface(sdf, options, grid=grid)` runs dual contouring on the
lattice, welds coincident vertices, and returns a `Surface`:

| field | what it is |
|---|---|
| `mesh` | The welded mesh: `vertices (V, 3)`, `faces (F, 3)` counterclockwise from outside, and `normals (V, 3)`, the field's own normal at each vertex. Each point is one vertex, so this is the mesh to index, export to STL, simplify or tet-mesh. |
| `corner_normals` | `(F, 3, 3)`: the shading normal at each triangle corner. On a smooth surface it is the vertex's own normal. On a crease or corner it is the normal of the side that triangle lies on. |
| `render_mesh()` | A `RenderMesh` of `vertices`, `normals`, `faces` and `rows`, with one vertex per smooth side. Crease and corner vertices are copied, and `rows` maps each copy back to `mesh`. This is what a renderer takes. |
| `feature_edges` | `(E, 2, 3)` segments along the part's creases and CSG seams. Empty unless `SurfaceOptions(feature_edges=True)`. |
| `clipped` | Whether the part reaches the lattice's faces, so the mesh is open there. When the whole lattice is inside the part, the mesh is also empty. |
| `grid`, `cell` | The lattice and its finest spacing. Walls and errors are counted in `cell`. |

`SurfaceOptions` has four knobs:

- `resolution` (64): cells along the longest axis, used when no grid is given.
- `sharp` (`True`): place crease and corner vertices exactly on the crease or
  corner.
- `simplify` (0): merge triangles while every changed triangle stays within
  this fraction of a cell of the field. Creases are kept, and `0.05` is a good
  value for a mesh you will turn into B-rep facets.
- `feature_edges` (`False`): also return the feature edges.

### Split normals at creases

`mesh.normals` holds one normal per vertex. On a crease that normal is the mean
of both sides, so a renderer that interpolates it shades a rim grainy.
`corner_normals` and `render_mesh()` split the normal instead. The sharp QEF
puts a crease cell's vertex on the crease, and the cell's Hermite normals, the
field's exact normals where the surface crosses the cell's edges, fall into one
cluster per smooth side. Normals within `CREASE_ANGLE` (30°) of each other are
on the same side. Each triangle corner then takes the normal of the side its
triangle faces.

On the clevis bracket at a 1.5 mm cell, the corners at split vertices are a
median 1° from their triangle's own normal, against 45° with the field
normals. A smooth part, such as a sphere, is not split at all. STL ignores
normals, and `save_obj` does not write them, so both export the welded `mesh`.

### Feature edges

The edges come from `lattice_feature_edges`, the same public classification the
viewer's overlay draws. It finds crease cells from the spread of their normals
and finds CSG seams where surface ownership flips between `min`/`max` operands.
It projects seam points onto the operands' common zero set and links the
feature cells along each curve. Every segment is a chord of the true curve,
with its ends on the surface. It is not a mesh edge: a curve crosses the
lattice diagonally, and mesh edges would trace a staircase around it.

A seam where two operands meet flush on one smooth face, such as a lug's stem
under its crown, is not drawn. Neither is a blended union, which has no edge.
The mesh is the same with or without `feature_edges`. The segment ends that
were projected onto a seam can sit a fraction of a cell off the facets, so
draw them with a depth offset. With the private tier installed, the viewer
draws exact B-rep edges instead; this call is the public lattice path.

## The checks

`mesh_topology(mesh)` reads the index graph and returns a `MeshTopology`:

- `open_edges`: edges that are not shared by exactly two triangles.
- `bodies`: connected pieces.
- `euler_characteristic`: 2 for each closed body, minus 2 for each hole through
  it.
- `watertight`: true when the mesh is closed and every edge is shared by
  exactly two triangles.

The clevis bracket reads `watertight`, 1 body, and Euler characteristic −14,
for its eight through-holes.

`wall_thickness(sdf, mesh, cell)` measures, against the field, the wall under
every vertex. From each vertex a ray runs into the material against the vertex
normal, sphere-traced until it leaves, then bisected onto the far face. A ray
counts only when it leaves through a face turned back at it, so a ray from
beside a convex edge does not pass for a thin wall. The function returns
`per_vertex` thicknesses (`nan` where a ray measured no wall), the `thinnest`
of them and the vertex `at` which it lies, `cells` (the thinnest wall in
cells), and `resolved` (the thinnest wall is at least `MIN_WALL_CELLS`). It
takes about 60 field evaluations, a fraction of a second.

| part | cell | thinnest wall | cells |
|---|---|---|---|
| clevis bracket (6 mm rib) | 1.5 mm | 5.74 mm | 3.8 |
| space-frame node (2 mm shell) | 1.0 mm | 1.97 mm | 2.0 |
| space-frame node | 1.5 mm | 1.06 mm | 0.7, not resolved |

Each check reports and refuses nothing. Whether a clipped part, an open mesh,
two bodies or a two-cell wall fails a build is the caller's decision.

## Migrating from 0.1.1's calls

A program pinned to `cadjoint==0.1.1` that called the mesher's stages
directly moves to the calls on this page:

| 0.1.1 | now |
|---|---|
| `fit_bounds` from `cadjoint.meshing.bounds`, then `GridSpec.from_bounds(origin, extent, ceil(extent / cell))` | `surface_grid(sdf, cell=cell)`, or `surface_grid(sdf, cell=cell, bounds=box)` with the caller's box. `fit_bounds` is exported from `cadjoint.meshing` too. |
| `extract_mesh(sdf, grid)` with the boundary warning filtered | `extract_surface(sdf, grid=grid).mesh`. The warning is gone, replaced by `Surface.clipped`. |
| `boundary_inside(sdf, grid)` | `Surface.clipped`, read from the samples the extraction already took. `boundary_inside` is still exported for a grid nothing was extracted on. |
| `remove_slivers(mesh)`, then dropping unused rows | Done inside `extract_surface`. `remove_slivers` stays public for other meshes. |
| Counting edges not shared by two triangles; a union-find for bodies | `mesh_topology(mesh)`. |
| Building a `Mesh` by hand for `simplify_mesh(mesh, sdf, error=cell / 20)` | `SurfaceOptions(simplify=0.05)`, or `simplify_mesh(surface.mesh, sdf, error=surface.cell / 20)`. |
| Splitting vertices at folds past 30° with area-weighted normals | `surface.render_mesh()`. The split follows the field's own Hermite normals, not the triangles' folds. |
| No feature edges for implicit parts | `SurfaceOptions(feature_edges=True)` and `surface.feature_edges`. |
| Sphere-tracing inward rays for the thinnest wall | `wall_thickness(sdf, surface.mesh, surface.cell)`, with `MIN_WALL_CELLS` and `WALL_CELLS`. |

`surface_grid(..., cell=)` lays the same lattice as the 0.1.1 recipe, and
`extract_surface` runs the same dual contouring on it, so the meshes are
unchanged: 59,484 triangles for the clevis bracket at a 1 mm cell.
